(على أنيابها) in the second line is the khabar of the doubled kaʾanna. Mizāj is that with which something else is mixed. What is meant by the canine teeth (anyāb) is the whole mouth, so it is figurative. Ghaḍḍ is the fresh and moist, and it is an adjective of an omitted noun qualified, i.e. "the taste of a fresh branch" [Translator's note: the text has «عضن», evidently for «غصن»]. Haṣr is bending a branch and inclining it towards you without breaking it off, in order to pluck its fruit; tahṣīr is an intensive of it. It is also narrated janāʾ instead of ijtināʾ, which is janā with the short ending, lengthened here by poetic necessity. Attributing the bending to the plucking is a rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī), of the kind of attribution to the cause. He likened her saliva to fine wine, and its taste to the taste of an apple whose branch the plucker bent in order to pluck it — an allusion that it has just now been plucked, no time having passed over it, and a hint likening his beloved to branches in delicacy, softness and swaying.
It has also been said that there is no inversion in the verse, and that the bāʾ is for transitivity like the hamza, the original being "that the keys would weigh down the strong band", i.e. burden them. This is also the view of the author of al-ʿUmda.
2- Hyperbole (al-mubālagha):
This is in the description of Qārūn's treasures, where He mentioned them in the plural and also pluralised the keys, and mentioned being weighed down, the band, and "possessors of strength". It is said that sixty mules carried the keys of his storehouses, each storehouse having a key. This hyperbole in the Qurʾān is among the finest and rarest of hyperboles in the view of the skilled: it is to exhaust everything that indicates abundance and to enumerate what relates to what he owns. Listen to ʿAmr ibn al-Ayham al-Taghlibī, how he wished to describe his people as generous and went on exhausting every quality he could manage, saying:
ونكرم جارنا ما دام فينا ... ونتبعه الكرامة حبث كانا
(We honour our neighbour as long as he is among us, and we send honour after him wherever he may be.) [Translator's note: the text has «حبث», evidently a misprint for «حيث».]
3- The eloquence of giving reasons (balāghat al-taʿlīl):
In His saying «إذ قال له قومه لا تفرح إن الله لا يحب الفرحين» there is a fine and beautiful giving of reason through the clause «إن الله لا يحب الفرحين», because pure joy in this world, insofar as it is this world, is blameworthy absolutely — and what joy is there in a thing that passes away and a shadow that shifts? Abū al-Ṭayyib glimpsed the sky of this eloquence in his splendid saying:
كأن الحزن مشغوف بقلبي ... فساعة هجرها يجد الوصالا
(It is as though grief were infatuated with my heart: the hour she forsakes me, it finds union.)
كذا الدنيا على من كان قبلي ... صروف لم يد من عليه حالا
(So was the world for those before me: vicissitudes that never kept one state for anyone.) [Translator's note: the text prints these two lines run together on one line, and «يد من» is evidently a misprint for «يدمن».]
أشد الغم عندي في سرور ... تيقّن عنه صاحبه انتقالا
(The worst grief, to me, lies in a joy from which its owner is certain he will be moved away.)
Do you not see how he made grief cling to his heart until it was as though it loved it passionately — but it does not join me except when she forsakes me, so when she forsakes me, grief joins my heart?
Then see how he urges abstinence from this world upon one granted joy and standing in it, because he knows it will pass away before long; and joy that its owner knows will soon withdraw from him is the worst grief. This is among the most eloquent and admonishing of speech and most indicative of the genius of the poet of immortality.
Among the beautiful things said on this meaning is the saying of Hudba ibn Khashram, when Muʿāwiya led him to al-Ḥarra to take retaliation from him for Ziyād ibn Zayd al-ʿUdhrī, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥassān ibn Thābit met him and asked him to recite, and he recited:
ولست بمفراح إذا الدهر سرني ... ولا جازع من صرفه المتقلب
(I am not one to rejoice much when Time pleases me, nor one to despair at its changing vicissitudes;)
ولا أبتغي شرا إذا الشر تاركي ... ولكن متى أحمل على الشر أركب
(nor do I seek evil when evil leaves me alone; but whenever I am driven to evil, I mount it.)
Mifrāḥ is one who rejoices much, and what is meant is denying joy at its root. The vicissitude of Time is its events. (إذا) is conditional, so a verb must follow it, i.e. "when Time pleases me" and "when evil is leaving me alone". (أحمل) is passive and (أركب) active; the first is the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ) and the second its answer and recompense.
4- Completion (al-tatmīm):
In His saying «ولا تنس نصيبك من الدنيا» there is an indispensable tatmīm, because if he did not seize the opportunity of this world to work for the Hereafter, he would have no portion in the Hereafter. In the ḥadīth:
"Seize five before five: your youth before your old age, your health before your sickness, your wealth before your poverty, your free time before your being busy, and your life before your death." Abū al-Ṭayyib returned and glimpsed the sky of this eloquence a second time, saying in an ode in which he lamented the mother of Sayf al-Dawla, who had died at Mayyāfāriqīn, the news of her death reaching him in Aleppo in the year three hundred and thirty-seven. Abū al-Ṭayyib recited his ode in Jumādā al-Ākhira of that year, and we present a choice selection of it:
نعد المشرفية والعوالي ... وتقتلنا المنون بلا قتال
(We make ready Mashrafī swords and lances, yet death kills us without a fight;)
وترتبط السوابق مقربات ... وما ينجين من خبب الليالي
(we tether swift steeds kept close at hand, yet they do not save us from the trotting of the nights.)
ومن لم يعشق الدنيا قديما ... ولكن لا سبيل إلى الوصال
(And who has not loved this world from of old? Yet there is no way to union with her.)
نصيبك في حياتك من حبيب ... نصيبك في منامك من خيال
(Your portion of a beloved in your life is your portion of a phantom in your sleep.)
رماني الدهر بالأرزاء حتى ... فؤادي في غشاء من نبال
(Time has shot me with calamities until my heart is in a sheath of arrows,)
فصرت إذا أصابتني سهام ... تكسرت النصال على النصال
(so that now, when arrows strike me, arrowheads break upon arrowheads.)
The intended illustration is in his saying نصيبك في حياتك… the line, i.e. a person's portion of union with his beloved in his life is like his portion of union with her phantom in his sleep; the point of likeness is the agreement of the two in the speed of their ending and their resemblance in the haste of their passing.

* Benefits:
1- The story of Qārūn:
Historians and storytellers have woven various narrations and wondrous legends around this unique story, which is fit to be the nucleus of a world drama representing the vanity that afflicts the wealthy. His lineage is disputed: it is said he was the paternal cousin of Moses son of ʿImrān, and it is said he was his maternal cousin. He is the first to have become proverbial for abundance of wealth. In His saying, Exalted is He, «وكان من قوم موسى» there is evidence of his faith and kinship. He was among the most handsome of people in face and in reciting the Torah, and he was called al-Munawwar (the illumined) for his beauty [Translator's note: the text has «لحسنة», evidently for «لحسنه»]. It is said that he was among the seventy whom Moses chose from his people. It is said that he went out riding a grey mule, with seven hundred maidservants on grey mules, wearing jewellery, fine robes and adornment, and he almost seduced the Children of Israel; then he transgressed, was arrogant and went headstrong until Allah destroyed him. The author of al-Munjid erred in claiming that he was Pharaoh's minister, as though he took him for Hāmān; this is among the results of haste and lack of verification. The cause of his destruction was that he envied Aaron for the ḥubūra. That is, when Moses crossed the sea and Pharaoh was drowned, he gave the ḥubūra to Aaron, so prophethood came to him. Ḥubūra, with ḍamma on the ḥāʾ, is leadership, taken from ḥabr in the sense of a chief in religion. Qārūn felt resentment at this and said: "Moses, you have the messengership and Aaron the ḥubūra, and I have nothing; I will not bear this." Moses said: "By Allah, I did not do that for Aaron; rather Allah gave it to him." He said: "By Allah, I will never believe you until you bring me a sign." So Moses ordered the chiefs of the Children of Israel that each man of them bring his staff. They brought them, and Moses threw them into a dome-tent of his — this was by the command of Allah — and Moses prayed that Allah would show them the evidence of that. They spent the night guarding their staffs, and in the morning Aaron's staff was quivering with green leaves on it, and it was of almond wood. Moses said: "Qārūn, do you not see what Allah the Exalted has done for Aaron?" He said: "By Allah, this is no more wondrous than the sorcery you do." Then he withdrew with those of the Children of Israel who were with him, and he had much wealth and many followers, so Moses prayed against him.
It is also said: When the verse of zakāt was revealed to Moses, Moses came to him and made terms with him for one dīnār out of every thousand dīnārs, and one sheep out of every thousand, and so on. He calculated it and found it a great amount. So he gathered his people of the Children of Israel and said: "Moses commands you in everything and you obey him, and now he wants to take your wealth." They said: "You are our elder, so command us as you wish." He said: "Bring me so-and-so the prostitute." He gave her a hundred dīnārs and ordered her to accuse Moses of [lying with] her. Then he came to Moses and said:
"Your people have gathered for you to command and forbid them." So he went out and stood among them preaching, and said: "Children of Israel, whoever steals, we will cut off his hand; whoever commits fornication, we will flog him, and if he has a wife, we will stone him." Qārūn cried out to him and said: "Even if it is you?" He said: "Yes." He said:
"The Children of Israel claim that you committed fornication with so-and-so the prostitute." He said: "Bring her to me." When she came, Moses said to her: "So-and-so, did I do what this man says?" She said:
"No, by Allah, Prophet of Allah; he only gave me a payment to accuse you of [lying with] me." So Moses fell prostrate, weeping and humbly beseeching, and Allah revealed to him: "Command the earth as you wish." He said: "Earth, take him!" It took him until it had made part of him disappear; then he kept saying "Take him!" while he was disappearing, until nothing of his body remained but a little, while he humbly beseeched Moses and implored him, and Moses kept saying "Take him!" until he disappeared. And so on to the end of this story, in which imagination expands and stretches to its furthest extent.
2- وي كأنه:
We promised you more of the discussion of «وي كأنه», so we say: al-Khalīl and Sībawayh held that «وي» is separate, meaning "I marvel"; then he began anew and said: كأنه لا يفلح الكافرون, and كأن here is not meant for likening but for decisiveness and certainty. On this is the verse of the Kitāb [of Sībawayh]:
وي كأن من يكن له نشب يجب ... ومن يفتقر يعش عيش حر
(Ah! It seems that whoever has wealth is loved, and whoever becomes poor lives a hard life.) [Translator's note: the verse is usually cited with «يحبب» and «عيش ضر»; translated as printed.]
Here he did not mean likening but certainty. Abū al-Ḥasan [al-Akhfash] held that ويك is separated from أنه. Yaʿqūb used to pause on ويك and then begin «أنه لا يفلح الكافرون», as though he meant by that to show that the kāf belongs to «وي», and that what is at its beginning is not «كأن» but «وي», as we mentioned, to which the kāf of address was added, as in ذلك and أولئك. This is supported by the saying of ʿAntara:
ولقد شفى نفسي وأبرأ سقمها ... قيل الفوارس ويك عنتر أقدم
(What healed my soul and cured its sickness was the horsemen's cry: "Ah, ʿAntar, charge!")
He brought it joined to the kāf without «أن», so it is a particle of address and not a noun in the genitive like that in غلامك and صاحبك, because «وي», when it is a verbal noun, follows the way of the verb and so is not put in construct for that reason. (أن) and what follows it is in the position of accusative by the verbal noun «وي», and that is why أن is given fatḥa; the implied form is "I marvel because the unbelievers do not prosper", and when the preposition dropped, the verb reached it directly and made it accusative. Al-Kisāʾī held that the original is «ويلك», the lām being dropped for lightness; this is far-fetched and there is no evidence for it. Some held that «ويكأنه» in its entirety [Translator's note: the text has «بكساله», evidently for «بكماله»] is a single noun, meaning the intensity of the joining and that its parts are not separated from one another.
The exact wording of Sībawayh is: "I asked al-Khalīl about His saying:
«ويكأنه لا يفلح» and about His saying «ويكأن الله», and he held that it is separated from «كأن», and that the meaning is that the people became aware and spoke according to their knowledge, or they were made aware and it was said to them: Does it not seem that this is so with you?"
Al-Aʿlam said: "The illustration is in his saying «ويكأن», which according to al-Khalīl and Sībawayh is composed of «وي», meaning alerting, with «كأن», which is for likening, and its meaning is 'have you not seen'; and on that the commentators interpreted it.
Some grammarians claimed that their saying «ويكأن» means 'woe to you, know that…', the lām being dropped from «ويلك», as ʿAntara said «ويك عنتر أقدم», and 'know' being omitted because the addressee knows it, together with frequency of use. This view is rejected because of the many changes it involves."
Abū Saʿīd al-Sīrāfī said: There are three views on «ويكأن». The first is al-Khalīl's view: «وي» is a word said by one who regrets, and said by one who makes another regret, and the meaning of «كأن» is certainty. The second is al-Farrāʾ's view: «ويك» is joined with the kāf and «أن» is separate, and its meaning according to him is affirmation, like your saying "do you not see?". The third view holds that «ويك» means «ويلك», and makes «أن» take fatḥa by an implied verb, as though he said: "Woe to you, know that Allah…".
Al-Farrāʾ said: «ويكأن» in the speech of the Arabs is affirmation, like a man's saying:
"Do you not see what Allah has done?" And the poet said: وي كأن من يكن له نشب (the line).
"A shaykh of the people of Basra told me: I heard a Bedouin woman say to her husband: 'Where is your son, woe to you?' He said: 'ويكأنه is behind the house', meaning: 'Do you not see him behind the house?' Some grammarians hold that they are two words, meaning:
«ويك، انه», intending «ويلك», with the lām dropped and أن given fatḥa by an implied verb, as though he said: 'Woe to you, know that he is behind the house', with 'know' implied. But we have not found the Arabs making verbs of supposing and knowing govern أن when implied, because such a verb loses its governing force when it is between the two parts or at the end; so when it is implied it is treated as left out. Do you not see that at the beginning it is not permissible to say 'O you, that you are standing' [with fatḥa], nor 'O you two, that…' [Translator's note: the text has «فمت», which appears corrupt], meaning 'I knew', 'I know', 'I thought' or 'I think'? As for dropping the lām from «ويلك» so that it becomes «ويك», the Arabs do say it because of its frequency in speech; ʿAntara said: ولقد شفى نفسي (the line). Others said that the meaning of «وي كأن» is that «وي» is separate, as when you say to a man «وي», meaning 'do you not see what is before you?' So he said: وي, then began anew كأن, meaning that Allah extends provision to whom He wills; and it is an exclamation, and كأن is in the manner of supposing and knowing. This is a sound view; but the Arabs did not write it separated, and had it been so they would have written it separated. It may be that it was used so frequently that it was joined to what is not part of it."
Abū al-Fatḥ Ibn Jinnī said: There are three views on «ويكأنه»:
- Some made it one word, and so did not pause on «وي».
- Some pause on «وي».
- Yaʿqūb pauses on «ويك», and it is the school of Abū al-Ḥasan.
"The view according to us is that of al-Khalīl and Sībawayh, namely that «وي» is a noun by which the verb is named, according to the analogy of their school; so it is as though it is a noun for 'I marvel'. Then he began anew and said «كأنه لا يفلح الكافرون», so «كأن» here is a statement stripped of the sense of likening, its meaning being that Allah extends provision; and «وي» is separate from «كأن». On this is the poet's saying: وي كأن من (the line). Among the instances in which «كأن» comes stripped of the sense of likening is the saying:
كأنني حين أمسي لا تكلمني ... متيم أشتهي ما ليس موجودا
(It is as if I, when evening comes and she does not speak to me, am one enthralled, longing for what does not exist.)
i.e. I, when evening comes, am enthralled, my state being thus and thus."
Al-Baghdādī said in Khizānat al-Adab: "As for Abū al-Fatḥ's saying that «وي» according to Sībawayh and al-Khalīl means 'I marvel', it is rejected; likewise his saying that «كأن» according to them is stripped of likening. As for his adducing a parallel for the absence of likening with the line:
كأنني حين أمسي (the line), that is the school of al-Zajjāj regarding the case where the khabar of «كأن» is a derived word: it is not then for likening, lest the thing likened and the thing it is likened to be identical. It has been answered that the khabar in such a case is omitted, i.e. 'as though I were an enthralled man', so it is for likening in accordance with its basic sense."
Al-Tabrīzī said in his commentary on the Muʿallaqāt: "As for his saying «ويك», some grammarians said it means ويحك and some said it means ويلك. Both views are wrong, because then it would have had to be read «ويك انه», just as one says ويلك انه and ويحك انه."
Al-Zamakhsharī said in his Kashshāf: "وي is separated from كأن; it is a word expressing awareness of error and regret. Its meaning is that the people became aware of their error in their wishing and their saying «يا ليت لنا مثل ما أوتي قارون», and regretted, then said «كأنه لا يفلح الكافرون», i.e. how much the situation resembles the fact that the unbelievers do not attain prosperity. This is the school of al-Khalīl and Sībawayh. He said:
وي كأن من يكن له نشب (the line).
Al-Farrāʾ related that a Bedouin woman said to her husband: 'Where is your son?' He said: 'وي كأنه is behind the house.' According to the Kufans, «ويك» means «ويلك», and the meaning is 'Do you not know that the unbelievers do not prosper?' It may be that the kāf is the kāf of address joined to «وي», as in his saying «ويك عنتر أقدم», and that أنه means لأنه, the lām stating that for the sake of which this was said; or 'because the unbelievers do not prosper, that happened', namely the swallowing up of Qārūn. Some people pause on وي and begin كأنه, and some pause on ويك."
The view of al-Shihāb al-Ḥalabī:
Al-Shihāb al-Ḥalabī, known as al-Samīn, who is very widely read, said: "وي كأنه: there are several schools on it:
The first: that وي is a word by itself, a verbal noun meaning 'I marvel', i.e. I [marvel]; the kāf is for causation, and أن and what falls within its scope is genitive by it, i.e. 'I marvel because Allah extends provision…'. The analogy of this is to pause on وي alone, and al-Kisāʾī did this.
The second: some said كأن here is for likening, except that its meaning has gone from it and it has become for statement and certainty; this too suits pausing on وي.
The third: that ويك is a word by itself, the kāf being a particle of address, and أن is governed by something omitted, i.e. 'know that Allah extends provision…'. Al-Akhfash said this. This suits pausing on ويك, and Abū ʿAmr did that.
The fourth: that its original is ويلك, the lām being dropped; this also suits pausing on the kāf, as Abū ʿAmr did.
The fifth: that ويكأن in its entirety is an independent, simple word meaning 'have you not seen?'; this may be transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Kisāʾī transmitted that it means 'Do you not see what Allah has done?', and Ibn Qutayba related that it means 'mercy be to you' in the dialect of Ḥimyar. It is written in the Qurʾān only as ويكأن and ويكأنه, joined, in both places; the generality of the readers followed the written form, while al-Kisāʾī paused on وي and Abū ʿAmr on ويك."
Ibn Hishām said in Awḍaḥ al-Masālik, with its commentary by Shaykh Khālid al-Azharī: "وا, وي and واها, all three mean 'I marvel', as in His saying, Exalted is He, «وي كأنه لا يفلح الكافرون»: وي is a verbal noun of the imperfect meaning 'I marvel', the kāf is a particle of causation, and أن is maṣdariyya and emphatic, i.e. 'I marvel at the unbelievers' not prospering'." This is what we chose in the i'rab, and we consider it the furthest from doubt and the nearest to correctness.

dervis-irab:33-37.t:
* Vocabulary:
(رِدْءاً): a helper. One says radaʾtuhu, "I helped him"; al-ridʾ is the name of that by which help is given, fiʿl in the sense of mafʿūl, just as al-difʾ is the name of that by which one is warmed. Salāma ibn Jandal said:
وردئي كل أبيض مشرفي ... شحيذ الحدّ عضب ذي فلول
(My help is every white Mashrafī sword, keen-edged, cutting, notched.)
That is: my help by which I guard myself against harms is every white sword. He expressed it with "every" because what is meant is to state the genus, not the individual. Mashrafī is a relation to Mashārif al-Yaman, which are villages of it; it is also said [that they are] of Syria. Shaḥīdh al-ḥadd: sharpened, from shaḥadha al-mudya, "he sharpened the knife". Al-ʿaḍb: the cutting one. Al-fulūl: the plural of fall, which is a break or notch in the edge of the sword, i.e. it has notches from striking battalions. Al-Naḥḥās said: One says radaʾtuhu and ardaʾtuhu.
(العضد): with fatḥa on the ʿayn and ḍamma on the ḍād, and with ḍamma, and with kasra: the thick part of the arm, from the elbow to the shoulder; its plural is aʿḍād and aʿḍud. It is the mainstay of the hand, and the hand is strong by its strength. Ṭarafa said — and it is also said [to be by] Aws ibn Ḥajar:
أبني لبيني لستمو بيد ... إلا يدا ليست لها عضد
(O sons of Lubaynā, you are not a hand — except a hand that has no upper arm.)
The ʿayn with the ḍād, as the first and second radicals of a word, have the special property of strength, hardness and extirpation. You say ʿaḍḍahu yaʿaḍḍuhu ʿaḍḍan: he gripped it with his teeth; one also says ʿaḍḍa bihi and ʿaḍḍa ʿalayhi. ʿAḍḍahu al-zamān: time was hard on him. Aʿaḍḍa al-sayfa bi-sāq al-baʿīr [he made the sword bite the camel's leg]; Labīd said:
ولكنا نعض السيف منها ... بأسوق عافيات الشحم كوم
(But we make the sword bite into their legs — high-humped, abounding in fat.)
And war bit him; al-Akhṭal said:
ضجوا من الحرب إذ عضت غواربهم ... وقيس عيلان من عاداتها الضجر
(They cried out against war when it bit their withers — and complaining is the habit of Qays ʿAylān.)
Mulk ʿaḍūḍ: oppressive kingship; from Abū Bakr: "After me you will see a biting kingship and a scattered community." Biʾr ʿaḍūḍ: a well of great depth, as though it bites the one drawing water by the hardship it puts upon him. ʿAḍabtuhu bi-lisānī: I reviled him; a man ʿaḍḍāb: a reviler. ʿAḍabtuhu ʿan ḥāja: I cut him off from a need; "what is it with you, cutting me off from what I am about?" Al-ʿaḍb: the cutting sword, and the man of sharp speech. ʿAḍbara al-kalb: the dog became like a lion. Al-ʿaḍbāra: a millstone, and a rock on which the fuller bleaches the cloth. Al-miʿḍād: a large butcher's knife with which bones are cut. Aʿḍala al-amr: the matter became severe; he has an incurable (ʿuḍāl) disease, which has baffled the physicians and defeated them. Dhū al-Iṣbaʿ married and came to his clan asking them for her dowry, but they refused him, so he said:
واحدة أعضلكم أمرها ... فكيف لو درت على أربع
(One wife's affair has baffled you — so how if I made the round of four?)
Fulān is a ʿuḍla, from al-ʿaḍal: a calamity among calamities. ʿAḍaltu ʿalā fulān: I constricted his affair and came between him and what he wanted; of it is «ولا تعضلوهن». He threw al-ʿaḍīha at him, i.e. slander. And he (upon him be peace) said: "There is no taʿḍiya against the heirs", i.e. harm shall not be brought upon them by dividing something like a sword or a ring.

* I'rab:
(قالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي قَتَلْتُ مِنْهُمْ نَفْساً فَأَخافُ أَنْ يَقْتُلُونِ): (رب) is the one addressed (munādā), in genitive construct with the omitted yāʾ of the speaker, as preceded. (إن) and its noun, and the clause (قتلت) is its khabar (predicate); (منهم) is a ḥāl (circumstantial), because it was originally an adjective and was placed before [its noun]; (نفسا) is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object). (فأخاف): the fāʾ is conjunctive, and (أخاف) is an imperfect verb, nominative (marfūʿ), its fāʿil (agent) latent (mustatir), its implied form being "anā"; (أن) and what falls within its scope is the object of (أخاف). (يقتلون) is accusative (manṣūb) by (أن), the sign of its accusative being the dropping of the nūn; the wāw is the agent, the nūn is for protection (wiqāya), and the omitted yāʾ of the speaker is the direct object. (وَأَخِي هارُونُ هُوَ أَفْصَحُ مِنِّي لِساناً فَأَرْسِلْهُ مَعِي رِدْءاً يُصَدِّقُنِي إِنِّي أَخافُ أَنْ يُكَذِّبُونِ): the wāw is conjunctive; (أخي) is a mubtadaʾ (subject), and (هارون) a badal (substitute) or ʿaṭf bayān (explicative apposition). (هو) is a mubtadaʾ and (أفصح) the khabar of (هو), and the clause is the khabar of (أخي). (مني) is attached (mutaʿalliq) to (أفصح), and (لسانا) is a tamyīz (specification). (فأرسله): the fāʾ is the faṣīḥa; (أرسله) is an imperative verb for supplication, its agent "anta", and the hāʾ is the direct object. (معي) is an adverb attached to (أرسله), and (ردءا) is a ḥāl. The meaning of the confirming will come in the section on rhetoric. (يصدقني) is an imperfect verb, nominative — had it been jussive, that would have been permissible, and it has been read so, as the answer to the request. The nūn is for protection and the yāʾ the direct object. The clause is resumptive, or an adjective of (ردءا), or a ḥāl from the object of (أرسله). The clause (إني أخاف) is a reason for what is requested: (إن) and its noun, and the clause (أخاف) is the khabar of (إن); (أن) and what falls within its scope is the object of (أخاف). (قالَ سَنَشُدُّ عَضُدَكَ بِأَخِيكَ وَنَجْعَلُ لَكُما سُلْطاناً): the clause (سنشد) is the object of the saying (maqūl al-qawl); the agent of (نشد) is "naḥnu", and (عضدك) is the direct object. (بأخيك) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (نشد). (نجعل) is conjoined to (سنشد); (لكما) is in the position of the accusative as the second object of (نجعل), and (سلطانا) is the first object of (نجعل), i.e. dominance and a clear proof; its explanation has passed in the section on vocabulary.
(فَلا يَصِلُونَ إِلَيْكُما بِآياتِنا أَنْتُما وَمَنِ اتَّبَعَكُمَا الْغالِبُونَ): the fāʾ is conjunctive; (لا) is negating; (يصلون) is an imperfect verb, nominative, and the wāw is the agent; (إليكما) is attached to (يصلون). As for (بآياتنا), it may be attached to the like of what it was attached to in «تسع آيات», i.e. "go with Our signs"; or to (نجعل); or to (يصلون); or to (سلطانا), i.e. "We give you both dominance by Our signs"; or to an omitted ḥāl; or [it may be] a redundant oath (laghw al-qasam). I see no reason requiring preference among these analyses, so choose from them whichever you consider preferable. (أنتما) is a mubtadaʾ; (من) is a relative noun conjoined to (أنتما); the clause (اتبعكما) is the ṣila (relative clause) of (من), and (الغالبون) is the khabar of (أنتما).
(فَلَمَّا جاءَهُمْ مُوسى بِآياتِنا بَيِّناتٍ قالُوا ما هذا إِلَّا سِحْرٌ مُفْتَرىً): the fāʾ conjoins to something omitted that the context requires. (لما) is a temporal adverb (ḥīniyya) or connective. (جاءهم موسى) is a verb, an object and an agent. (بآياتنا) is attached to (جاءهم) or to an omitted ḥāl, and (بينات) is a ḥāl, i.e. clear in their indication. The clause (قالوا) is the apodosis of (لما). (ما) is negating, (هذا) is a mubtadaʾ, (إلا) is a particle of restriction, (سحر) is the khabar and (مفترى) an adjective.
(وَما سَمِعْنا بِهذا فِي آبائِنَا الْأَوَّلِينَ): the wāw is conjunctive; (ما) is negating; (سمعنا) is a verb and its agent; (بهذا) is attached to (سمعنا); (في آبائنا) is a ḥāl from (هذا), so it is attached to something omitted, its implied form being "kāʾinan" (being); (الأولين) is a naʿt (adjective) of (آبائنا). (وَقالَ مُوسى رَبِّي أَعْلَمُ بِمَنْ جاءَ بِالْهُدى مِنْ عِنْدِهِ): (ربي) is a mubtadaʾ and (أعلم) its khabar; (بمن) is attached to (أعلم); the clause (جاء بالهدى) is the ṣila of (من), and (من عنده) is a ḥāl. (وَمَنْ تَكُونُ لَهُ عاقِبَةُ الدَّارِ إِنَّهُ لا يُفْلِحُ الظَّالِمُونَ): the wāw is conjunctive, and (من) is conjoined to the first (من). (تكون) is a defective imperfect verb; (له) is its fronted khabar and (عاقبة الدار) its postponed noun. The noun of (تكون) may also be the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn) or the pronoun of the story, with (له) a fronted khabar and (عاقبة الدار) a postponed mubtadaʾ, the clause being the khabar of (تكون). It may also be complete (tāmma), in which case the clause (له عاقبة الدار) is a ḥāl and the agent of (تكون) is a pronoun referring to (من). (إن) and its noun, and the clause (لا يفلح الظالمون) is its khabar.

* Rhetoric:
1- Figurative attribution (al-isnād al-majāzī):
In His words «فأرسله معي ردءا يصدقني» there is a figurative attribution, for confirming has been attributed to him because he is its cause. The meaning of figurative attribution is that confirming literally belongs to the one who confirms, so attributing it [to him] is literal; there is no confirming in the cause, but the attribution was borrowed for it because it is engaged with the confirming by way of causation, just as the agent is engaged with it by way of direct action. The proof of that is His words «إني أخاف أن يكذبون». The purpose of his words (يصدقني) is not that he should say "you have spoken the truth", or say to the people "my brother has spoken the truth"; rather, the way of his confirming him is that he should set out the truth concisely with his tongue, dispute with the disbelievers with his eloquence, establish the argument and adduce the proof supported by figures, as the articulate man of ready eloquence does. Do you not see His words «وأخي هارون هو أفصح مني لسانا»? In this is a proof of the loftiness and nobility of eloquent expression and its superiority over ordinary speech, which does not hit the mark nor penetrate to the depths of souls.
2- Majāz mursal (synecdoche/metonymic trope):
In His words «سنشد عضدك بأخيك» there is a majāz mursal by way of stating the cause and meaning the effect, in two stages, one following the other: the strength of the upper arm is a cause that entails the strength of the hand, and the strength of the hand entails the strength of the person, at the second stage. Al-Shihāb, in his gloss on al-Bayḍāwī, chose that it be an allusive kināya (kināya talwīḥiyya); he said: "Al-shadd is strengthening, so it is either an allusive kināya for strengthening him, because the hand is strengthened by the strengthening of the upper arm, and the whole [person] is strengthened by the strengthening of the hand; or it is a representative metaphor (istiʿāra tamthīliyya), likening Moses' state in being strengthened by his brother to the state of the hand in being strengthened by the upper arm." And that is not far-fetched.

dervis-irab:83-88.t:
* I'rab:
(تِلْكَ الدَّارُ الْآخِرَةُ نَجْعَلُها لِلَّذِينَ لا يُرِيدُونَ عُلُوًّا فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلا فَساداً وَالْعاقِبَةُ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ): resumptive speech, set out to show that the Hereafter has been prepared for those who do not desire exaltation in the earth. (تلك) is a mubtadaʾ (subject); (الدار) is a badal (substitute) from the demonstrative; (الآخرة) is an adjective of (الدار); the clause (نجعلها) is the khabar (predicate) of (تلك); (للذين) are attached (mutaʿalliq) to (نجعلها) as its second object; the clause (لا يريدون) is the ṣila (relative clause) of (الذين); (علوا) is the object of (يريدون); (في الأرض) is an adjective of (علوا); (ولا فسادا) is conjoined to (علوا); (العاقبة) is a mubtadaʾ and (للمتقين) the khabar. (مَنْ جاءَ بِالْحَسَنَةِ فَلَهُ خَيْرٌ مِنْها): resumptive speech, set out to promise the doers of good and threaten the doers of evil, after mentioning that the outcome belongs to the God-fearing. (من) is a conditional noun that makes jussive, in the position of nominative as mubtadaʾ; (جاء) is a past verb in the position of jussive as the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ); (بالحسنة) are attached to (جاء); the fāʾ links the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) because it is a nominal clause; (له) is a khabar put first and (خير منها) a mubtadaʾ put after; the clause is in the position of jussive as the apodosis; and the verb and the answer together are the khabar of (من).
(وَمَنْ جاءَ بِالسَّيِّئَةِ فَلا يُجْزَى الَّذِينَ عَمِلُوا السَّيِّئاتِ إِلَّا ما كانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ): conjoined to what precedes. (يجزى) is a passive imperfect verb; (الذين) is the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent); the clause (عملوا السيئات) is the ṣila of the relative; (إلا) is a particle of restriction; (ما) is the second object of (يجزى); the clause (كانوا) is the ṣila; and the clause (يعملون) is the khabar of (كانوا). (إِنَّ الَّذِي فَرَضَ عَلَيْكَ الْقُرْآنَ لَرادُّكَ إِلى مَعادٍ): (إن) and its noun; the clause (فرض) is the ṣila; (عليك) are attached to (فرض); (القرآن) is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object). The meaning of "He imposed the Qurʾān upon you" is: He made its recitation and conveyance obligatory upon you. The lām is the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa); (رادك) is the khabar of (إن), and the kāf is in the position of genitive by the construct (iḍāfa); (إلى معاد) are attached to (راد) because it is an active participle. Its indefiniteness indicates matters that will come in the section on rhetoric.
(قُلْ رَبِّي أَعْلَمُ مَنْ جاءَ بِالْهُدى وَمَنْ هُوَ فِي ضَلالٍ مُبِينٍ): (ربي) is a mubtadaʾ and (أعلم) its khabar; it is in the sense of ʿālim (knowing), and that is why it governs (من) in the accusative; the clause (جاء) is the ṣila [Translator's note: the text runs these together as «نصب من جملة جاء صلة», evidently «نصب من، وجملة جاء صلة»]; (بالهدى) are attached to (جاء); (من) is conjoined to the first (من); (هو) is a mubtadaʾ, (في ضلال) its khabar and (مبين) its adjective. (وَما كُنْتَ تَرْجُوا أَنْ يُلْقى إِلَيْكَ الْكِتابُ إِلَّا رَحْمَةً مِنْ رَبِّكَ): the wāw is a conjunction; (ما) is negating; (كنت) is kāna and its noun, and the clause (ترجو) is its khabar; (أن) and what falls within its scope is the object of (ترجو); (إليك) are attached to (يلقى); (الكتاب) is the deputy agent; (إلا) is a particle of restriction in the sense of lākin, for rectification (istidrāk); (رحمة) is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose); and (من ربك) is an adjective of (رحمة). It is also permissible for the exception to be in its proper state, i.e. connected (muttaṣil), but understood according to the sense. (فَلا تَكُونَنَّ ظَهِيراً لِلْكافِرِينَ): the fāʾ is the fāʾ al-faṣīḥa (the fāʾ that discloses an implied condition); (لا) is prohibitive; (تكونن) is an incomplete imperfect verb in the jussive (majzūm) by the prohibitive (لا), the sign of its jussive being the dropping of the nūn, and the wāw is its noun, and the kāf is the direct object [Translator's note: so in the text; this description (dropped nūn, wāw, kāf) fits «يصدنك» below rather than «تكونن», whose noun is the latent «أنت»]; the said nūn is the heavy nūn of emphasis; (ظهيرا) is the khabar of (تكونن); and (للكافرين) are attached to (ظهيرا). (وَلا يَصُدُّنَّكَ عَنْ آياتِ اللَّهِ بَعْدَ إِذْ أُنْزِلَتْ إِلَيْكَ): conjoined to what precedes. The i'rab of its like has preceded, but we repeat it because of a slight difference. (لا) is prohibitive; (يصدنك) is an imperfect verb in the jussive by the prohibitive (لا), the sign of its jussive being the dropping of the nūn. The wāw was dropped because, when the nūn was dropped, two quiescent letters met, the wāw and the assimilated nūn, so the wāw was dropped because it is weak and there is evidence indicating it, namely the ḍamma; its original form is yaṣuddūnaka. (عن آيات الله) are attached to (يصدنك); the adverb is attached to an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial); (إذ) is an adverb for the past, put in construct with one like it — nouns of time are put in construct with إذ, as in your saying ḥīnaʾidhin and yawmaʾidhin, and this has been discussed before; the clause (أنزلت) is in the position of genitive through the adverb being put in construct with it; and (إليك) are attached to (أنزلت). (وَادْعُ إِلى رَبِّكَ وَلا تَكُونَنَّ مِنَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ): the wāw is a conjunction; (ادع) is an imperative verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on the dropping of the weak letter, and the agent is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "you"; (إلى ربك) are attached to (ادع); (لا) is prohibitive; (تكونن) is in the jussive by it — its i'rab has preceded — and its noun is latent, its implied form being "you"; and (من المشركين) is its khabar.
(وَلا تَدْعُ مَعَ اللَّهِ إِلهاً آخَرَ لا إِلهَ إِلَّا هُوَ): the wāw is a conjunction; (لا) is prohibitive; (تدع) is an imperfect verb in the jussive by (لا); the agent is latent, its implied form being "you", referring to Muḥammad ﷺ — the address is to him but someone else is meant, after the pattern of His saying «لئن أشركت ليحبطن عملك». (مع الله) is an adverb of place attached to (تدع); (إلها) is the direct object and (آخر) a naʿt (adjective) of (إلها). (لا إله إلا هو): its i'rab has preceded, and the clause is in the position of accusative as a ḥāl. (كُلُّ شَيْءٍ هالِكٌ إِلَّا وَجْهَهُ لَهُ الْحُكْمُ وَإِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ): (كل) is a mubtadaʾ; (شيء) is the muḍāf ilayhi; (هالك) is the khabar of the mubtadaʾ; (إلا) is a particle of exception and (وجهه) is the excepted — the meaning of the exception will come in the section on rhetoric. (له) is a khabar put first and (الحكم) a mubtadaʾ put after; (إليه) are attached to (ترجعون); (ترجعون) is a passive imperfect verb, and the wāw is the deputy agent.

* Rhetoric:
1- The secret of the indefiniteness in His saying «إلى معاد» is magnification, as though this place of return had been prepared for you to the exclusion of other human beings. It has been said that what is meant by it is Mecca, namely the day of the Conquest; a man's maʿād is his town, because he departs from it and returns to it, so maʿād on this view is a noun of place. It is narrated that when he ﷺ left the cave by night, he travelled off the road for fear of pursuit; then when he returned to the road and halted at al-Juḥfa, between Mecca and Medina, and recognised the road to Mecca, longing leapt in his breast, yearning for his homeland stirred him, and he longed for his birthplace and the birthplace of his forefathers. So it was revealed to him to reassure his heart. In it the measure of longing for homelands is manifest. All the poets have glimpsed the sky of this meaning. Ibn al-Rūmī said:
بلد صحبت به الشبيبة والصبا ... ولبست ثوب العيش وهو جديد
(A land in which I kept company with youth and boyhood, and wore the garment of life while it was new;)
فإذا تمثل في الضمير رأيته ... وعليه أغصان الشباب تميد
(whenever it takes shape in my mind I see it with the branches of youth swaying over it.)
And Abū Tammām said:
نقل فؤادك حيث شئت من الهوى ... ما الحب إلا للحبيب الأول
(Move your heart wherever you will in love: true love is only for the first beloved.)
كم منزل في الأرض يألفه الفتى ... وحنينه أبدا لأول منزل
(How many dwellings on earth a young man grows fond of, yet his longing is ever for the first dwelling.)
What has been said on love of homelands is much. Among what confirms what we have said about love of homelands is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, «ولو أنا كتبنا عليهم أن اقتلوا أنفسكم أو اخرجوا من دياركم ما فعلوه إلا قليل منهم», where He put killing themselves on a level with leaving their homes; and He said, Exalted is He: «وما لنا أن لا نقاتل في سبيل الله وقد أخرجنا من ديارنا وأبنائنا».
One of them said: "Among the signs of the intelligent man are his kindness to his brothers, his longing for his homelands, and his courtesy to the people of his time."
A Bedouin was asked: "What do you do in the desert when the summer heat becomes intense and everything wears its shadow as a sandal?" He said: "And is life anything but that? One of us walks a mile and streams with sweat; then he sets up his staff, throws his cloak over it and sits in its shade, measuring out the breeze, and it is as though he were in the hall of Chosroes."
Yaḥyā ibn Ṭālib al-Ḥanafī, one of the poets of the ʿAbbāsid state, said:
ألا هل إلى شم الخزامى ونظرة ... إلى قرقرى قبل الممات سبيل
(Is there any way, before death, to smelling the lavender and one glance at Qarqarā,)
فأشرب من ماء الحجيلاء شربه ... يداوى بها قبل الممات عليل
(so that I may drink a draught of the water of al-Ḥujaylāʾ by which a sick man is cured before death?)
فيا أثلات القاع قلبي موكل ... بكن وجدوى خيركنّ قليل
(O tamarisks of the plain, my heart is devoted to you, though the gift of your good is little;)
ويا أثلات القاع قد مل صحبتي ... مسيري فهل في ظلكنّ مقيل
(O tamarisks of the plain, my companions have wearied of my journeying: is there a midday rest in your shade?) [Translator's note: the text prints these two lines run together on one line.]
أريد انحدارا نحوها فيردّني ... ويمنعني دين عليّ ثقيل
(I wish to go down towards her, but a heavy debt upon me turns me back and holds me.)
أحدث نفسي عنك إذ لست راجعا ... إليك فحزني في الفؤاد دخيل
(I talk to myself of you, since I am not returning to you, and my grief has entered deep into my heart.)
And the famous lines of al-Ṣimma al-Qushayrī:
تمتع من شميم عرار نجد ... فما بعد العشية من عرار
(Enjoy the scent of the ʿarār of Najd, for after this evening there is no ʿarār.)
ألا يا حبذا نفحات نجد ... وريا روضة بعد القطار
(How lovely are the breezes of Najd, and the fragrance of a meadow after the rain,)
وعيشك إذ يحل الحي نجدا ... وأنت على زمانك غير زار
(and your life when the tribe camps in Najd and you find no fault with your time.)
شهور ينقضين وما شعرنا ... بأنصاف لهن ولا سرار
(Months pass and we notice neither their middles nor their last nights;)
فأما ليلهن فخير ليل ... وأقصر ما يكون من النهار
(as for their nights, they are the best of nights, and the shortest of days.)
What we have presented now suffices us.
2- Synecdochic metaphor (al-majāz al-mursal):
In His saying, Exalted is He, «كل شيء هالك إلا وجهه», i.e. except Him, it is of the kind of mentioning the part and intending the whole; it has been the custom of the Arabs to express the whole by its noblest part.

dervis-irab:38-42.t:
* Vocabulary:
(أَطَّلِعُ): al-ṭulūʿ and al-iṭṭilāʿ: ascending. One says ṭalaʿa al-jabala and iṭṭalaʿa with one meaning. "Your soul is ṭulaʿa toward this matter" and "it yaṭṭaliʿu toward it", i.e. it yearns.
(الْمَقْبُوحِينَ): al-maqbūḥ: the one driven away; qabaḥahu Allāh: He drove him away. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "Qabuḥa the thing, qubḥan, so it is qabīḥ, of the pattern of qaruba, and it is the opposite of ḥasan (beautiful). Qabaḥahu Allāhu yaqbaḥuhu, with two fatḥas: Allah removed him from good. In the Revelation: «وهم من المقبوحين», i.e. those kept far from success. The doubled form is for intensification; and qabbaḥa ʿalayhi fiʿlahu taqbīḥan [he denounced his deed as ugly]."
Abū Zayd said: Qabaḥa Allāhu fulānan qabḥan and qubūḥan: He removed him far from every good. Abū ʿAmr said: qabaḥtu wajhahu, without doubling, in the sense of qabbaḥtu, with doubling. Like it are the poet's words:
ألا قبح الله البراجم كلها ... وقبح يربوعا وقبح دارما
(May Allah make ugly the Barājim, all of them, and make ugly Yarbūʿ, and make ugly Dārim.)

* I'rab:
(وَقالَ فِرْعَوْنُ يا أَيُّهَا الْمَلَأُ ما عَلِمْتُ لَكُمْ مِنْ إِلهٍ غَيْرِي): the wāw conjoins to something implied that the context requires, i.e. "and Pharaoh said, after he had gathered the sorcerers to oppose him, and there happened between them and Moses what happened". (يا) is a vocative particle, and (أيها) is the one addressed (munādā), an intended indefinite noun (nakira maqṣūda), indeclinable (mabnī) on ḍamma in the position of the accusative; the hāʾ is for alerting, and (الملأ) is a badal (substitute). (ما) is negating; (علمت) is a verb and its fāʿil (agent); (لكم) is a ḥāl (circumstantial). (من) is a redundant (zāʾida) preposition, and (إله) is genitive in wording by (من) and accusative in position, because it is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object); (غيري) is a naʿt (adjective) of (إله).
(فَأَوْقِدْ لِي يا هامانُ عَلَى الطِّينِ فَاجْعَلْ لِي صَرْحاً): the fāʾ is the faṣīḥa; (أوقد) is an imperative verb, its agent latent (mustatir), its implied form being "anta". (يا) is a vocative particle, and (هامان) is a singular proper-name munādā. (على الطين) is attached (mutaʿalliq) to (أوقد). (فاجعل) is conjoined to (أوقد); (لي) is in the position of the accusative as the second object of (اجعل), and (صرحا) is the first object. (لَعَلِّي أَطَّلِعُ إِلى إِلهِ مُوسى وَإِنِّي لَأَظُنُّهُ مِنَ الْكاذِبِينَ): (لعل) and its noun, and the clause (أطلع) is its khabar (predicate); (إلى إله موسى) is attached to (أطلع). (وإني): the wāw is conjunctive; (إن) and its noun; the lām is the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa), and the clause (أظنه) is the khabar; the hāʾ is the first object and (من الكاذبين) is in the place of the second object. (وَاسْتَكْبَرَ هُوَ وَجُنُودُهُ فِي الْأَرْضِ بِغَيْرِ الْحَقِّ): conjoined to (وقال فرعون). (هو) is the agent of (استكبر), or a tawkīd (emphasis) of the agent, because the latency of the agent in the third person is permissible. (جنوده) is conjoined to (هو); (في الأرض) is attached to (استكبر), and (بغير الحق) is a ḥāl from the agent of (استكبر), i.e. "clothed in what is other than the truth".
(وَظَنُّوا أَنَّهُمْ إِلَيْنا لا يُرْجَعُونَ): (ظنوا) is conjoined to (استكبر); (أن) and what follows it take the place of the two objects of (ظنوا). (إلينا) is attached to (يرجعون); (لا) is negating, and the clause (لا يرجعون) is the khabar of (أن). (فَأَخَذْناهُ وَجُنُودَهُ فَنَبَذْناهُمْ فِي الْيَمِّ فَانْظُرْ كَيْفَ كانَ عاقِبَةُ الظَّالِمِينَ): (فأخذناه) is conjoined to what preceded; (أخذناه) is a verb, its agent and its direct object. (جنوده) is conjoined to the hāʾ in (أخذناه), or is a mafʿūl maʿahu (object of accompaniment). (فنبذناهم) is conjoined to (فأخذناه), and (في اليم) is attached to (نبذناهم). (فانظر): the fāʾ is the faṣīḥa, and (انظر) is an imperative verb; (كيف) is the fronted khabar of (كان), and (عاقبة الظالمين) its postponed noun. (وَجَعَلْناهُمْ أَئِمَّةً يَدْعُونَ إِلَى النَّارِ وَيَوْمَ الْقِيامَةِ لا يُنْصَرُونَ): (جعلناهم) is a verb, its agent and the first object; (أئمة) is the second object, and the clause (يدعون) is an adjective of (أئمة); (إلى النار) is attached to (يدعون). (ويوم القيامة): the wāw is conjunctive, and (يوم القيامة) is an adverb attached to (ينصرون); (لا) is negating, and (ينصرون) is a passive imperfect verb. You may also make the wāw circumstantial and the clause a ḥāl.
(وَأَتْبَعْناهُمْ فِي هذِهِ الدُّنْيا لَعْنَةً): (أتبعناهم) is conjoined to what preceded; (في هذه الدنيا) is a ḥāl, (الدنيا) is a badal from (هذه), and (لعنة) is the second object.
(وَيَوْمَ الْقِيامَةِ هُمْ مِنَ الْمَقْبُوحِينَ): the adverb is attached to something omitted indicated by His word (المقبوحين), as though it were said "and they will be made ugly on the Day of Resurrection". We implied an omitted element only because attaching it to (المقبوحين), which is the apparent [analysis], is prevented by the presence of the relative al-; however, they have allowed latitude in that and attached it to what [al-] governs, and there is nothing to prevent that. You may also conjoin it to the position of (في هذه الدنيا), i.e. "and We made a curse follow them on the Day of Resurrection". (هم) is a mubtadaʾ (subject) and (من المقبوحين) its khabar.

* Rhetoric:
In His words «فأوقد لي يا هامان على الطين» there is an exquisite iṭnāb (amplification). That is, He did not say "bake bricks for me", in order to avoid mentioning the word ājurr (baked brick), because its composition — despite the ease of its pronunciation — is not eloquent, and that is a matter that taste alone determines. Do you not see this word where it occurs in a verse of al-Nābigha al-Dhubyānī from his ode rhyming in dāl, whose beginning is:
من آل مية رائح أو مغتدي ... عجلان ذا زاد وغير مزود
(Departing from the family of Mayya in the evening or the morning, in haste, with provisions or without?)
The verse is:
أو دمية من مرمر مرفوعة ... بنيت بآجر يشاد بقرمد
(Or a marble statue raised up, built of baked brick plastered with lime.)
The word ājurr in the verse is unsettled and jarring because of its commonness. If you want to learn something of the secret of the eloquence the Qurʾān contains, look at this place: when mention of baked brick was brought in, He did not mention it by its word, nor by the word qarmad either; rather it was mentioned in the Qurʾān in another way, expressing baked brick as kindling upon clay (al-ẓīn «[Translator's note: so printed; read al-ṭīn, "clay".]»). Moreover, this expression better matches the eloquence of the Qurʾān and its lofty rank, and more closely resembles the speech of tyrants. And his commanding Haman — his vizier and second — to kindle upon clay, calling him by his name with "yā" in the middle of the speech, is a sign of self-aggrandisement and tyranny. This expression has encompassed many of the expressions of insolent tyrants, in the following way:
1- He called his vizier with the vocative particle.
2- He placed his call in the middle of the command and the building of the tower.
3- His hope of looking up to Allah.
4- The stupidity that clings to insolent tyrants, since they fall into contradiction without realising it. A moment before he had declared «ما علمت لكم من إله غيري», expressing the negation of the thing known by negation of knowledge and announcing his determination to deny; then he soon announced his hope of looking up [to Him]. So was he determined to deny or was he not?
A section on the choice of words:
The scholars of bayān have given attention to the word and the secret of its choice. The gist of what is said about it is that the beauty and ugliness of words is a matter that goes back to taste alone: what it finds beautiful is beautiful and what it finds ugly is ugly; usage is not a proof of beauty. This is a path on which one unacquainted with its ways goes astray. Whoever does not know the craft of verse and prose, and the effort its practitioner finds in fashioning and choosing words, is excused in saying what he said:
لا يعرف الشوق إلا من يكابده ... ولا الصبابة إلا من يعانيها
(None knows longing but the one who endures it, nor passion but the one who suffers it.)
And al-Ṣāḥib ibn ʿAbbād, who was among those infatuated with Abū al-Ṭayyib, and who used to use his poetry in his writings and quote from it — when estrangement arose between him and Abū al-Ṭayyib al-Mutanabbī because the latter disdained to answer him. They mention that al-Ṣāḥib Abū al-Qāsim hoped that al-Mutanabbī would visit him in Isfahan and treat him as he treated those he sought out among the chiefs of the age; he was at that time a young man and had not yet become vizier. Al-Ṣāḥib wrote to him, courting him in inviting him and guaranteeing to share all his wealth with him; but al-Mutanabbī gave him no weight, did not answer his letter and did not fulfil his wish. After that al-Mutanabbī went to the court of ʿAḍud al-Dawla in Shiraz, and his journey resulted — as Abū Manṣūr al-Thaʿālibī says in Yatīmat al-Dahr — "in the attainment of the wish, and the arrival at the watering-place of death". That is, al-Mutanabbī was killed upon leaving him, laden with gifts and presents.
Al-Thaʿālibī said: "Al-Ṣāḥib took him as a target at which he shot the arrows of disparagement, tracking his lapses and slips in his poetry and decrying his faults, while he was the best acquainted of people with his merits, the one who knew them best by heart, and the one who used them most and quoted them most in his discourses and letters."
Al-Ṣāḥib composed an epistle on what he faulted in al-Mutanabbī. If we suppose that what prompted al-Ṣāḥib to compose this epistle was his displeasure with al-Mutanabbī for being too proud to praise him, we nonetheless find that he did not unjustly attack him in anything in it, did not wrong him in a single letter of it, faulted him only with what is a fault, and could not get at him except by way of words alone. We cite here samples from this epistle.
1- Al-Ṣāḥib faulted al-Mutanabbī for affecting eloquence with anomalous words. Of that are his words:
أيفطمه التوراب قبل فطامه ... ويأكله قبل البلوغ إلى الأكل
(Does the dust wean him before his weaning, and eat him before he reaches the age of eating?)
He said: "I do not see how he fell in love with al-tawrāb until he made it the amulet of his poems." Al-tawrāb is dust. The meaning of the verse: Does the dust wean him before his mother weans him, and does the dust eat him before he reaches the age of eating?
2- He faulted him for the word turunj in his words:
شديد البعد من شرب الشمول ... ترنج الهند أو طلع النخيل
(Far removed from drinking wine are the citron of India and the spathes of the palm.)
Al-Ṣāḥib said sarcastically: "I do not know whether the opening of the verses is finer, or the meaning more original, or his word turunj more eloquent." Al-Ṣāḥib was right, for the eloquent form is utrujj and utrujja; from it is the ḥadīth: "The likeness of the believer who reads the Qurʾān is that of the citron (utrujja): its scent is good and its taste is good." Abū Zayd reported turunj and turunja. Abū al-Ṭayyib says: The citron of India and the palm spathes are far removed from your station in wine-drinking, even if others take them for that, because such a state is not supposed of you; you bring them, and the like of them among fragrant plants, only to enjoy their beauty.
3- Al-Ṣāḥib criticised the plural ākhāʾ in his poetry, where he said:
كل آخائه كرام بني الدنيا ولكنه كريم الكرام
(All his brothers are the noble ones of this world's sons, but he is the noblest of the noble.)
He said: "Had al-ākhāʾ occurred in the rāʾ-ode of al-Shammākh it would have been found heavy; so how much more with verses such as:
قد سمعنا ما قلت في الأحلام ... وأنلناك بدرة في المنام
(We have heard what you said in dreams, and We gave you a purse of money in sleep.)
When speech is not harmonious, its critics pronounce it counterfeit and its assayers declare it spurious."
In this way he goes on exposing the faults of al-Mutanabbī, all of them matters that go back to the word alone. Much of it will come up with us, so let us be content with what we have mentioned of it now.
The critics also faulted entangled rhymes. They faulted Abū Tammām for his rhyme in thāʾ in his ode whose opening is:
قف بالطلول الدارسات علاثا ... أصخت حبال قطينهن رثاثا
(Stop at the effaced ruins, O ʿUlātha; the ropes of their dwellers have become worn.)
«[Translator's note: «أصخت» is as printed; the sense requires «أضحت», "have become", which the gloss follows.]»
ʿUlāthā is a truncated (murakhkham) munādā; its original is "yā ʿUlātha". They faulted Abū al-Ṭayyib for his rhyme in shīn in his ode whose opening is:
مبيتي من دمشق على فراش ... حشاه لي بحرّ حشاي حاش
(My night's lodging near Damascus is on a bed whose stuffer has stuffed it for me with the heat of my innards.)
And they faulted Ibn Hāniʾ al-Andalusī for his rhyme in khāʾ in his ode whose opening is:
سرى وجناح الليل أقتم أفتخ ... حبيب ضجيع بالعبير مضمّخ
(A beloved bedfellow, perfumed with ʿabīr, travelled by night while the wing of night was dark and outspread.)
Al-aqtam: the dark; al-aftakh: the elongated.
What has preceded is enough for us, for we have almost taken the book out of its subject.

dervis-irab:43-46.t:
* Vocabulary:
(بَصائِرَ): al-baṣīra: reason, perspicacity, a lesson, a witness and a proof. One says "his limbs are baṣīra against him", i.e. witnesses; and "a firāsa (physiognomic insight) possessing baṣīra", i.e. true. The plural is baṣāʾir. His words «بصائر للناس» mean lights for their hearts by which they perceive realities and distinguish between truth and falsehood, after they had been altogether blind to understanding and perception. So al-baṣīra is the light of the heart by which one gains insight, just as al-baṣar is the light of the eye by which one sees. More of its meaning will come in the section on i'rab.
(ثاوِياً): residing. One says thawā yathwī, of the pattern of ḍaraba, thawāʾan and thawiyyan al-makāna, and fīhi and bihi: he resided [in the place]; and thawā al-rajul: the man died. ʿAbīd ibn al-Abraṣ said at the opening of his Muʿallaqa «[Translator's note: so in the source; this ode opening «آذنتنا ببينها أسماء» is usually attributed to al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza.]»:
آذنتنا ببنيها أسماء ... رب ثاو يملّ منه الثواء
(Asmāʾ has announced to us her departure — many a dweller there is whose dwelling grows wearisome.)
«[Translator's note: «ببنيها» is as printed; the familiar text reads «ببينها», "her departure", which the gloss follows.]»

* I'rab:
(وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنا مُوسَى الْكِتابَ مِنْ بَعْدِ ما أَهْلَكْنَا الْقُرُونَ الْأُولى): the wāw is resumptive; the lām is the answer to the omitted oath; (قد) is a particle of realisation. (آتينا) is a verb and its fāʿil (agent); (موسى) is the first object and (الكتاب) the second object. (من بعد) is attached (mutaʿalliq) to (آتينا); (ما) is maṣdariyya; (أهلكنا) is a verb and its agent; (القرون) is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object), and (الأولى) is an adjective. (بَصائِرَ لِلنَّاسِ وَهُدىً وَرَحْمَةً لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَذَكَّرُونَ): (بصائر) is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from (الكتاب), or a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose). On the circumstantial view a muḍāf must be implied, i.e. "possessing insights", or it is by way of hyperbole. (للناس) is a naʿt (adjective) of (بصائر); (هدى ورحمة) are conjoined to (بصائر). (لعلهم يتذكرون): (لعل) and its noun, and the clause (يتذكرون) is its khabar (predicate). (وَما كُنْتَ بِجانِبِ الْغَرْبِيِّ إِذْ قَضَيْنا إِلى مُوسَى الْأَمْرَ وَما كُنْتَ مِنَ الشَّاهِدِينَ): the wāw is conjunctive or resumptive; (ما) is negating; (كنت): (كان) and its noun; (بجانب) is its khabar, and (الغربي) is a muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct), i.e. "and you were not, O Muḥammad, at the side of the western mountain"; so it is a case of omitting the qualified noun and putting the adjective in its place. Al-Zajjāj chose this. Al-Kalbī said: at the side of the western valley, i.e. where Moses held intimate converse with his Lord. (إذ) is an adverb for the past, attached to the [notion of] being-located to which the preposition and its genitive noun are attached; the clause (قضينا) is genitive by the adverb's being put in construct with it, and (الأمر) is the direct object. The wāw is a conjunction; (ما) is negating; (كنت): (كان) and its noun, and (من الشاهدين) its khabar. The matter decreed is the revelation that was revealed to him.
(وَلكِنَّا أَنْشَأْنا قُرُوناً فَتَطاوَلَ عَلَيْهِمُ الْعُمُرُ): the wāw is conjunctive; (لكن) and its noun, and the clause (أنشأنا) is its khabar; (نا) is the agent and (قرونا) the direct object. (فتطاول) is conjoined to (أنشأنا); (عليهم) is attached to (تطاول), and (العمر) is the agent. (وَما كُنْتَ ثاوِياً فِي أَهْلِ مَدْيَنَ تَتْلُوا عَلَيْهِمْ آياتِنا وَلكِنَّا كُنَّا مُرْسِلِينَ): the wāw is conjunctive; (ما) is negating; (كنت): (كان) and its noun, and (ثاويا) its khabar; (في أهل مدين) is attached to (ثاويا). The clause (تتلو) is in the place of the accusative as a second khabar of (كنت), or a ḥāl from the pronoun in (ثاويا). (ولكنا): the wāw is circumstantial or conjunctive; (لكن) and its noun, and the clause (كنا) is its khabar; (كان) and its noun, and the clause (مرسلين) «[Translator's note: so in the source, "the clause"; (مرسلين) is a single word.]» is its khabar.
(وَما كُنْتَ بِجانِبِ الطُّورِ إِذْ نادَيْنا وَلكِنْ رَحْمَةً مِنْ رَبِّكَ): the wāw is conjunctive; (ما) is negating; (كنت): (كان) and its noun; (بجانب) is the khabar of (كنت), and (الطور) is a muḍāf ilayhi. The adverb is attached to the [notion of] being-located to which the khabar, namely (بجانب), is attached. The address in the two verses is to Muḥammad ﷺ, i.e. "you were not present at the place in which We revealed to Moses (upon him be peace), nor were you among the witnesses of the revelation, nor were you at the side of the Mount when We called him to take the Torah". The clause (نادينا) is in the position of the genitive by the adverb's being put in construct with it. (ولكن): the wāw is conjunctive, and (لكن) is a particle of rectification (istidrāk), inoperative because it has been lightened. (رحمة) is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi, i.e. "We sent you and taught you all this as a mercy", and (من ربك) is an adjective of (رحمة). (لِتُنْذِرَ قَوْماً ما أَتاهُمْ مِنْ نَذِيرٍ مِنْ قَبْلِكَ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَذَكَّرُونَ): (لتنذر): the lām is of reason, and (تنذر) is an imperfect verb, accusative (manṣūb) by an optionally concealed (أن) after the lām of reason; the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to the omitted "We sent you". The object of purpose was put in the genitive with the lām only because the agent differs. (قوما) is the direct object; (من) is a redundant (zāʾida) preposition, and (نذير) is genitive in wording and nominative in position as the agent; (من قبلك) is an adjective of (نذير). (لعل) and its noun, and the clause (يتذكرون) is its khabar.

* Rhetoric:
1- Jinās al-taḥrīf (paronomasia by vowelling):
In His words «ولكنا كنا مرسلين» there is jinās al-taḥrīf, in which the vowelling is what distinguishes the two words or parts of them. Parallels to it have passed and many parallels will pass. An example of it in poetry is the words of Abū al-ʿAlāʾ al-Maʿarrī:
والحسن يظهر في شيئين رونقه ... بيت من الشعر أو بيت من الشعر
(Beauty shows its splendour in two things: a verse of poetry (shiʿr) or a tent of hair (shaʿar).)
And also his:
لغيري زكاة من جمال فإن تكن ... زكاة جمال فاذكري ابن سبيل
(To others belongs alms from camels (jimāl); but if there is to be alms from beauty (jamāl), remember the wayfarer.)
The paronomasia in the first is between «الشعر» and «الشعر», and in the second between «جمال» and «جمال». How delicate are the words of Bahāʾ al-Dīn Zuhayr:
زها ورد خديك لكنه ... بغير النواظر لم يقطف
وقد زعموا أنه مضعف ... وما علموا أنه مضعفي
(The rose of your cheeks bloomed, but it is plucked by nothing but the eyes. They claimed it was doubled (muḍaʿʿaf, a double rose), not knowing that it is what weakens me (muḍʿifī).)
2- Ishāra (allusion):
The study of this device has preceded more than once, and we take it up now in expanded form, as we also take up symbolism, which has become widespread in the modern age, so that our book may be comprehensive of the varieties of literature. As for the allusion in the verse, it is what the word «الأمر» alluded to in His words «وما كنت بجانب الغربي إذ قضينا إلى موسى الأمر». It alluded to the beginning of Moses' prophethood, the Real's addressing him, and His giving him the clear signs — throwing the staff so that it became a serpent, bringing out his hand white, sending him to Pharaoh, and his asking that his arm be strengthened by his brother Aaron — and everything that took place at that station. Topics like these, if a researcher pursued them, would be beyond counting in the Mighty Book.
Allusion in poetry:
We have presented poetic samples of this device. Qudāma holds that the best verse in allusion is the words of Zuhayr:
وإني لو لقيتك فاجتمعنا ... لكان لكل مندية لقاء
(Were I to meet you and we came together, every shameful thing would meet its match.)
He alluded to him [thereby] the ugliness of what he would do if he met him. Al-Ḥātimī recited, from ʿAlī ibn Hārūn, from his father, from Ḥammād, from his father Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm al-Mawṣilī:
جعلنا السيف بين الخدّ منه ... وبين سواد لمته عذارا
(We made the sword a cheek-strap between his cheek and the black of his locks.)
He alluded to the form of the blow with which he struck him, without mentioning it, a subtle allusion indicating its manner; he was only describing that they struck his neck. Among the kinds of allusion are tafkhīm (magnification) and īmāʾ (hinting). Tafkhīm is like the words of Allah the Exalted «الحاقة ما الحاقة», and the words of Kaʿb ibn Saʿd al-Ghanawī:
أخي ما أخي لا فاحش عند بيته ... ولا ورع عند اللقاء هيوب
(My brother — what a brother! Not foul-spoken at his home, nor faint-hearted and timid at the encounter.)
Īmāʾ is like the words of the Exalted «فغشيهم من اليم ما غشيهم»: He hinted at what covered them and left out the explanation; mention of it has preceded under the heading of ibhām (vagueness). Kuthayyir, the lover of ʿAzza, said:
تجافيت عني حين لا لي حيلة ... وخلفت ما خلفت بين الجوانح
(You turned away from me when I had no recourse, and left behind what you left behind between my ribs.)
His words "and left behind what you left behind" are a charming hint.
Among the kinds of allusion is ramz (symbol), as in the words of one of them describing a woman whose husband was killed and who was taken captive:
عقلت لها من زوجها عدد الحصى ... مع الصبح أو مع جنح كل أصيل
(I paid her, as blood-money for her husband, the counting of pebbles at dawn or at the onset of every evening.)
He means: I gave her neither blood-money nor retaliation for her husband, except the grief that drives her to count pebbles. The root meaning of al-ʿaql is taking blood-money; (عدد الحصى) is the object of (عقلت). Its origin is from the words of Imruʾ al-Qays:
ظللت ردائي فوق رأسي قاعدا ... أعد الحصى ما تنقضي عبراتي
(I remained sitting, my cloak over my head, counting pebbles; my tears do not cease.)
He means that when he came to the abodes of the tribe and found no one, he put his cloak over his head and sat thinking, counting pebbles, his tears not drying. Of charming symbol are the words of Abū Nuwās describing cups of mixed wine bearing engraved images; mention of these verses has preceded, and of them here:
قرارتها كسرى وفي جنباتها ... مها تدّريها بالقسيّ الفوارس
(At its bottom is Chosroes, and on its sides wild cows that horsemen stalk with bows.)
فللخمر ما زرّت عليه جيوبها ... وللماء ما دارت عليه القلانس
(To the wine belongs what their collars are buttoned over, and to the water what their caps encircle.)
He says: the limit of the wine, on the figures of these horsemen that are in the cups, is up to the collarbones and the throats; and water was added to it as a mixture, so the drink reached above their heads. It may also be that the bubbles reached that place when it was mixed and foamed, but the first is more charming. Its point is knowing its level pure from knowing its level mixed. This, in their view, is something in which Abū Nuwās had no predecessor.
Symbolism in modern poetry:
The rise of symbolism was a reaction against realism, which went to excess in being influenced by science and in distancing itself from poetic imagination. Just as realism was able to dislodge romanticism from its position, the rise of symbolism heralded the retreat of realism, with that new movement, which occupied the last quarter of the nineteenth century, taking its place.
Poetry for the adherents of this school is — as one of them says — "an ecstasy and a dream that carry a person into the realm of the unconscious, where he glimpses there realities he cannot see by way of reason and logic in the conscious world. He does not find in the inner world fully clear images that he can express explicitly, but he expresses them by symbol, so that he can suggest to the reader the same feeling and transport him to the same state."
From here came the obscurity of symbolism. Then they went further into vagueness and wrapped poetry in a wrapping of fog: they dropped the particles of simile and relied on the word for their suggestion, deliberately placing it before or after its position so that it would increase its suggestive radiations. They likewise matched letters with colours and colours with meanings: red symbolises tumultuous life, blood, the lust of love and storms; green represents the cosmos, nature and the sea; blue represents setting out to what lies beyond cosmic matter, where there is the world of angels and music that reaches the depths; violet is the colour of mystical visions; yellow is for sadness and the striving toward a better world; and white reveals calm, tranquillity and purity. Baudelaire, the French symbolist poet, expresses the relationship between colours, scents and sounds in his poem in which he treats the unity of nature, saying: Nature is a temple with living pillars, from which obscure words sometimes issue; man passes through forests of symbols that gaze at him with familiar looks.
And the long, distant echoes of obscurity mingle in a dark, deep unity, vast as the night and as the light, and scents, colours and sounds answer one another. What we have cited is enough for us; whoever wants more, let him refer to what has been written on this subject, and it is much.
3- Iḥtirās (precaution):
In this same verse is the device of iḥtirās, mention of which has preceded often. Perhaps the iḥtirās that occurs in this verse is the most wonderful iḥtirās in the Qurʾān. The address, as we said, is directed to the Messenger ﷺ. When He (Blessed and Exalted) negated of His noble Messenger his being at the place where He decreed the matter to His interlocutor Moses, He defined the place as the western side and did not describe it as the right [side], as He said in relating about Moses (upon him be peace): «وناديناه من جانب الطور الأيمن» — out of courtesy on His part, Glorified is He, toward His Prophet, [avoiding] negating of him his being on the right side. And He, Glorified is He, described the side there as the right one, since He related that He called His interlocutor Moses from it, honouring him.
It must be pointed out, moreover, that in His words «بجانب الغربي» the original is that it be an adjective, i.e. "at the western side"; but it was turned away from that and made an adjective of something omitted, necessarily, because of the impossibility of putting the qualified noun in genitive construct with the adjective, since the adjective is the qualified noun in meaning, and putting a thing in construct with itself is an error. The implied form is "the side of the western place".
